title: From 43% to 78%: How We Got Here and Why We’re Not There Yet
author: Erin Sharon
summary: A reading specialist traces how her school moved kindergarten benchmark attainment from 43% to 78% in two years after her district adopted UFLI Foundations for K-2. Her central move is to reframe the problem as a Tier 1 failure rather than an intervention failure, so that effort goes into prevention before remediation. She then refuses to settle at 78%, arguing that the remaining 22% signals work still to do. Drawing on MTSS resources from Brown and Stollar and from Hanlin and Montgomery, she turns to implementation fidelity, naming pacing, connected phonation, blendable sounds, alternating encoding and decoding, and connected text as the routines most often varied. She closes by shifting from student-level to systems-level decision-making with the data. The piece is a practitioner case study that pairs a concrete data story with a checklist for tightening core literacy instruction.
points: Intervening a way out of what is really a Tier 1 problem is unsustainable, so the author reorients her role toward prevention in kindergarten classrooms.
Embedding 30 minutes a day of modeling and support inside each kindergarten classroom coincided with benchmark attainment rising from 43% to 73% and then 78%.
Fidelity matters even within a good program: pacing, connected phonation, blendable sounds, alternating encoding and decoding, and keeping decodable text are the specific routines she flags.
Citing Brown and Stollar, she argues that when more than 20% of students are below grade level, the response must be systems-level improvement rather than more student-level intervention.
Progress-monitoring spelling assessments should guide small-group instruction rather than function as graded spelling tests.
quotes: I jam-packed my schedule, wrote my goals around first grade, purchased my own UFLI Foundations manual, and did everything I could to intervene my way out of what was really a Tier 1 problem.
On a podcast, I heard Stephanie Stollar say, “Prevention is the best intervention,” and that has been my motto ever since.

I think 43% to 78% in two years is great! But after learning more about reading outcomes and MTSS through invaluable resources like It’s Possible (Hanlin & Montgomery, 2024), MTSS for Reading Improvement (Brown & Stollar 2025), and joining the Reading Science Academy, I’m now seeing that 78% meeting benchmark means 22% of students are not achieving that success, and I’m not okay with settling for that.

It’s important to remember that each lesson is only intended to be 30 minutes per day. If you do every word in the blending drill and word work section, and dictate all 3 sentences for students to write, you’ll never get through in 30 minutes, especially in kindergarten.
UFLI recommends (and research supports) using connected phonation in your lessons - that is, stretching out each sound and then blending, “/mmmaaaap/. . . map.

They point out that when more than 20% of students are performing below grade level, the intervention system is likely to be overwhelmed and not very effective, and they recommend using data to inform “system-level” decisions (Brown & Stollar, 2025).

The progress monitoring spelling assessments are meant to guide your small group instruction. They’re not meant to be used as a spelling test that is graded and sent home, and remember, mastery is not expected immediately after each concept is introduced!
